For a partial order \(P\) of width \(w\), some chain family \(\mathcal{C}\) of \(w\) chains has \({\preceq_{\mathcal{C}}} = {\preceq_{\mathcal{M}, P}}\).
Every chain family with fewer chains differs from \(P\) on some pair of decisions.

• a chain may rank requirements that the order leaves incomparable, as the dashed links show
  • all chains in \(O(|\mathcal{M}|^2 \log |\mathcal{M}|)\) time, then a genetic algorithm for chain families (Lai et al. 2020) optimizes over \(\mathcal{C}\)

• a more important metric gets a faster-growing weight, and weights of the same growth form a layer
  • the layers refine \(P\): metrics comparable in \(P\) are still comparable
made-up landings \(\textcolor{gray}{x = (u, v)}\): each requirement drawn holds exactly on its set

• the optima \(x_1, x_2, x_4, \ldots\) of the weighted sums tend to a limit \(x_0\)
  • \(x_0\) holds glide cone and soft touchdown, and no landing that holds both is better on the next layer, in green

The limit \(x_0\) zeroes as many of the first layers as any decision can.
Among the decisions that zero those first layers, \(x_0\) is Pareto optimal on the next layer.

• here no landing holds glide cone, soft touchdown and the whole next layer together
  • the limit holds tilt limit and speed limit as well, and leans 21.9° near touchdown
The limit can lose in the next layer
\(x_0\) and \(\textcolor{dpgreen}{c}\): same tilt limit and upright

• the weighted optima \(x_i\) tend to \(x_0\), which is Pareto optimal on tilt limit and upright
  • but \(c\) has the same values on both and is better on target: the limit need not be optimal for \(P\)
  • on a finite \(\mathcal{X}\), the limit is always optimal for \(P\)

• a layered extension of \(P\): each layer an antichain, each union \(B_1 \cup \cdots \cup B_l\) an upper set
  • its weights grow by one power of \(i\) per layer
\(\mathcal{B}\) = ({glide cone, soft touchdown}, <font color="#008000">{tilt limit, speed limit, upright}</font>, \(\ldots\))

• \(\mathcal{B}\) targets an upper set \(U\) if \(U = B_1 \cup \cdots \cup B_l\) and \(B_{l+1} = \operatorname{Max}(\mathcal{M} \setminus U)\)
  • if \(U\) can hold, but not with the whole next layer, the limit holds \(U\) and is Pareto optimal on the next layer
  • here the limit also holds tilt limit and speed limit, and the limit of another extension holds upright in place of tilt limit
Targeting every upper set to get the maximally zeroed ones

• the green weights give the layers ({soft touchdown}, {upright}, {glide cone}), which target {soft touchdown, upright}
  • no extension targets two of \(\emptyset\), {soft touchdown}, {glide cone} and {soft touchdown, upright}, so four are needed
Targeting every upper set to get the maximally zeroed ones

The width of \(\sqsubseteq\) is the smallest number of layered extensions that together target every upper set but \(\mathcal{M}\).
This width is at most \((|\mathcal{M}| + 1)^w - 1\).
Here the width is 4, against the bound 15.

• the green weights give the layers ({soft touchdown}, {upright}, {glide cone}), which target {soft touchdown, upright}
  • no extension targets two of \(\emptyset\), {soft touchdown}, {glide cone} and {soft touchdown, upright}, so four are needed
  • on the order of the case study: 7 extensions, against the bound \((8 + 1)^3 - 1 = 728\)

For convex \(\mathcal{X} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) and convex metrics, the minimal layered extensions together give \(\mathcal{X}^*_P = \bigcup_{\mathcal{B}} \mathcal{X}^*_{\mathcal{B}}\).
A family that misses one of them misses an optimal decision of some such problem.

Let \(\mathcal{X} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) be convex and every metric be \(\max\{f_m, 0\}\) with \(f_m\) strictly convex.
Then every family that targets every upper set gives \(\mathcal{X}^*_P\).

If \(d\) is posetally improving at \(x\), then \(x + t d \prec_{\mathcal{M},P} x\) for every small enough \(t > 0\).

• an oracle gives, for each metric \(m\) at \(x\), a cone \(C_{m,x}\) of directions that do not worsen \(m\), and whether it strictly improves \(m\)
  • \(d\) is posetally improving if some metric improves, and each metric whose cone misses \(d\) is strictly below an improving one
  • every \(d\) comes with an upper set \(U\) that certifies the posetal improvement

Take differentiable metrics and the gradient oracle.
Then \(x\) admits a posetally improving direction if and only if some \(d\) has \(\nabla m(x)^\top d < 0\) for every maximal metric \(m\).

• for differentiable metrics, a posetal descent is steepest descent on the maximal metrics (Fliege and Svaiter 2000)
  • the maximal metrics here are glide cone and soft touchdown
Strictly convex metrics: no improving direction means optimal
• if some \(y\) were better than \(x\), the direction from \(x\) toward \(y\) would improve \(x\) posetally
Strictly convex metrics: no improving direction means optimal

Let every metric \(m\) be \(\max\{f_m, c_m\}\) with \(f_m\) strictly convex.
Then \(x \in \mathcal{X}^*_P\) if and only if \(x\) admits no posetally improving direction.

• convex is not enough: for incomparable \(m_1 = x_1^2\), \(m_2 = x_2^2\), \((0, 1)\) admits no improving direction, yet \((0, 0)\) is better
  • for differentiable strictly convex metrics, the accumulation points of steepest descent on the maximal metrics lie in \(\mathcal{X}^*_P\)
